Newly hatched nestlings of the American dusky flycatcher (Empidonax oberholseri) emerge at a remarkably modest mass of 1.2 grams [Wwb = 1.2 grams], a value consistent with the altricial developmental strategy typical of tyrant flycatchers. This neonatal body weight, recorded from freshly hatched chicks in the field, underscores the substantial parental investment required to bridge the gap to independence. Eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and hatching occurs after approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days], a developmental period that aligns closely with incubation durations reported for other Empidonax species. The relatively short incubation phase, combined with the low hatchling mass, suggests a trade-off between rapid embryonic development and the energetic costs of yolk provisioning. Once hatched, the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on biparental feeding, with both adults making frequent visits to deliver arthropod prey. This initial stage of life is critical for establishing the growth trajectory that will ultimately determine the chick’s survival and future reproductive potential.

Under the thermal regime typical of the active metabolic season for this species (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), a predictable sequence of developmental milestones governs the transition to independence. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs just 17 days after hatching [tx = 17 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid nestling period is comparatively brief among insectivorous passerines of similar body size, reflecting an adaptive strategy to minimize exposure to nest predators in montane environments. During this phase, the nestling undergoes a dramatic increase in body mass, ultimately approaching the adult asymptotic mass of 11 grams [Wwi = 11 grams] by the time of fledging. The capacity to nearly decuple birth weight in just over two weeks highlights the efficiency of parental provisioning and the high metabolic rate sustained by the developing chick. Post-fledging, the young bird remains dependent on its parents for an additional period as it refines its foraging skills and builds the fat reserves necessary for migratory preparation.

Gonadal maturation in the American dusky flycatcher follows a considerably slower schedule than the initial growth phase. Puberty, defined by the onset of functional gametogenesis, is attained at 51 days after hatching [tp = 51 days after hatching] when maintained at an active metabolic body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This post-fledging developmental interval encompasses the critical transition from a dependent nestling to a nutritionally independent juvenile capable of sustained flight and self-feeding. The attainment of reproductive maturity at this age is relatively late compared to the fledging date, indicating that substantial somatic growth and behavioral maturation must occur before the reproductive system is activated. Juveniles during this period undergo a complete pre-formative molt, acquiring the adult plumage that is essential for both thermoregulation and social signaling. Field observations suggest that young birds delay dispersal from natal territories until after this physiological milestone is reached, likely benefiting from continued access to familiar foraging grounds while completing their development.

The long-term life history strategy of the American dusky flycatcher is characterized by a conservative reproductive schedule. The time since birth at first brood, or the age at which a female initiates her first successful nesting attempt, is 365 days [tR = 365 days] under the standard thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This deferred first reproduction, occurring in the second calendar year of life, is a common pattern among migratory passerines that return to breeding grounds with limited time for territory establishment and mate acquisition. Females produce only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = a single clutch per year], with typical clutch sizes ranging from three to four eggs [N_R_i = three to four eggs]. This low annual fecundity rate is offset by high nest attentiveness and a relatively extended breeding season, allowing for replacement clutches if the initial attempt fails due to predation or inclement weather. The combination of delayed maturity and low reproductive output suggests that adult survival and territory fidelity are critical components of the species’ demographic persistence.

Maximum lifespan records for the American dusky flycatcher, derived from both field banding studies and museum specimen data, indicate that the oldest documented individuals survive for approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] when measured at the typical active metabolic body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity is notable for a small-bodied insectivore and implies a relatively low extrinsic mortality rate, likely facilitated by the species’ migratory behavior, which reduces exposure to year-round predation pressure. The extended lifespan, combined with low annual reproductive output (a single clutch per year [F_R_i = a single clutch per year]), aligns with a slow pace-of-life syndrome commonly observed in tropical and subtropical passerine lineages, suggesting that this montane-breeding species has converged on a similar life history strategy despite its temperate distribution. Adult survival between breeding seasons is influenced by the quality of wintering habitat in Central America, where individuals must maintain body condition through the non-breeding period. These demographic parameters collectively point to a population regulated more by adult survival rates than by fecundity, a pattern typical of long-lived bird species with low annual reproductive investment.
